title: The Conquest of Makkah
subtitle: The Friday of Liberation, the Four Columns of Entry, and the Humility of the Prophet
summary: On Friday, the twentieth of Ramadan in the eighth year of the Hijrah, the Muslim army advanced into Makkah through four coordinated columns. Meeting negligible resistance aside from a brief localized skirmish in the southern sector, the Prophet entered his native city riding his camel Al-Qaswa, bowing his head so low in humble gratitude that his beard brushed the saddle. Proceeding to the Kaaba, he circumambulated the Ancient Sanctuary, declaring the eternal triumph of truth over falsehood.

sections.text: The Four Tactical Columns of Entry

At dawn on Friday, the twentieth of Ramadan in the eighth year of the Hijrah, the Muslim army mobilized from Dhu Tuwa to enter Makkah. To prevent bloodshed and secure every approach simultaneously, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided his forces into four coordinated tactical columns. Khalid ibn al-Walid commanded the right flank comprising bedouin allies, entering from Lower Makkah (Kuda) in the south. Al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam commanded the left flank, advancing from the north through Kada. Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah led the central infantry down the main valley corridor, while Qays ibn Sa'd advanced along the western ridge.

The Prophet issued strict standing orders to all commanders: 'Do not fight anyone unless they initiate combat against you.' The advance was remarkably peaceful. Three columns entered the city without facing a single arrow. Only in Khalid's sector in the south did a small band of diehard pagan rejectionists—led by Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, Safwan ibn Umayyah, and Suhayl ibn Amr—gather at Khandamah to mount resistance. After a brief and sharp skirmish, the opposition collapsed; approximately twelve combatants fell, while two Muslims (Karz ibn Jabir and Khunays ibn Khalid) were martyred after straying from their unit. Khalid quickly secured the southern gate and restored order.
The Supreme Humility of the Victorious Prophet

While worldly conquerors traditionally entered vanquished capitals with haughty pride, triumphant fanfares, and vengeful retribution, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ presented the world with an unmatched spectacle of sublime humility. Riding his favorite camel Al-Qaswa, draped in a black turban, the Prophet bowed his head so low in devotion and tearful gratitude to Allah that the tips of his blessed beard brushed the wooden pommel of his saddle.
As his camel stepped gracefully into the valley, his lips moved continuously in recitation of the opening verses of Surah Al-Fath:

إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ فَتْحًا مُبِينًا * لِيَغْفِرَ لَكَ اللَّهُ مَا تَقَدَّمَ مِنْ ذَنْبِكَ وَمَا تَأَخَّرَ وَيُتِمَّ نِعْمَتَهُ عَلَيْكَ وَيَهْدِيَكَ صِرَاطًا مُسْتَقِيمًا
'Indeed, We have granted you a clear triumph, that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin and what will follow and complete His favor upon you and guide you to a straight path.' (Surah Al-Fath 48:1–2)
Circumambulating the Kaaba and the Vanishing of Falsehood

The Prophet proceeded straight to the Sacred Mosque, surrounded by the Muhajirun and Ansar. Dismounting near the Kaaba, he began the circumambulation upon his mount, touching the Black Stone with his bent wooden staff (al-mihjan). Arrayed around the ancient sanctuary stood 360 stone and wooden idols, which the tribes of Arabia had worshipped for centuries.

With his staff, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pointed to each idol in succession, striking them until they toppled face-down upon the dust, while declaring the immortal Quranic proclamation recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari:

جَاءَ الْحَقُّ وَزَهَقَ الْبَاطِلُ إِنَّ الْبَاطِلَ كَانَ زَهُوقًا
'Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is bound to vanish.' (Surah Al-Isra 17:81; Sahih al-Bukhari 4287)

And he added from Surah Saba: 'Truth has arrived, and falsehood can neither originate anything nor repeat it.' (Surah Saba 34:49). One by one, the false gods of Arabia crumbled upon the sacred stones, restoring the primordial sanctuary built by Prophet Ibrahim to the uncompromised worship of the One Creator.

The entry into Makkah was not merely a military triumph; it was the definitive moral and spiritual transformation of Arabian civilization. The city that had persecuted the early believers, martyred Sumayyah and Yasir, starved the Muslims in the Mountain Pass of Abu Talib, and orchestrated relentless wars against Madinah was now peacefully reconciled under the banner of divine mercy.

With the perimeter secured and the Kaaba liberated, the Prophet stood before the people of Makkah, preparing to deliver a historic address that would redefine justice and forgiveness for all generations to come.
